name: Fuunji
description: Legendary tsukemen (dipping ramen) shop with an almost permanent queue. The rich, creamy fish and pork broth is absurdly good. Many consider this the best tsukemen in Tokyo.
whatToOrder: Tsukemen (dipping noodles) with ajitama (seasoned egg). Get the large size.
tips: Expect 30-60 min wait. Use the ticket machine. Eat quickly - noodles get cold. Add the soup-wari (broth) to your dipping sauce at the end to drink it.

name: Ichiran Shibuya
description: The famous solo-dining ramen chain with individual booths separated by partitions. Customize every aspect of your tonkotsu ramen on a paper form. A quintessential Tokyo experience.
whatToOrder: Classic tonkotsu ramen. Customize richness, garlic, spice on the order form. Add extra noodles (kaedama) for ¥210.
tips: Open 24 hours - great late night option. Use the vending machine to buy your ticket first. The Shibuya location rarely has long waits late at night.

name: Afuri Ebisu
description: Famous for their yuzu shio (citrus salt) ramen - a lighter, more refined bowl compared to heavy tonkotsu. The yuzu aroma hits you before the first sip. Beautiful, modern interior.
whatToOrder: Yuzu Shio Ramen is the signature. The vegan ramen is also excellent.
tips: Ticket machine ordering. Multiple locations but Ebisu original is the best. Less of a wait than Fuunji.

name: Rokurinsha Tokyo Station
description: Located in Tokyo Station's Ramen Street. Famous for incredibly thick, rich tsukemen with chewy noodles. The broth is like a concentrated seafood-pork bomb.
whatToOrder: Tsukemen with all toppings. The morning ramen set (before 10am) has shorter lines.
tips: Arrive before 11am or after 2pm to avoid the worst queues. Located in the Yaesu side underground First Avenue area.

name: Mutekiya
description: Ikebukuro institution serving rich tonkotsu ramen with a loyal following. The broth is creamy and deeply flavored from long hours of simmering pork bones. Open very late.
whatToOrder: Tonkotsu ramen with chashu and ajitama.
tips: Open until 4am - perfect post-drinking ramen. The line moves fast despite looking long.

name: Nakiryu
description: One of only two Michelin-starred ramen shops in the world. The tantanmen (spicy sesame ramen) is extraordinarily complex - layers of chili, sesame, Sichuan pepper, and umami.
whatToOrder: Tantanmen (spicy sesame ramen) is the star. The shoyu ramen is also excellent.
tips: Arrive by 10:30 to queue before opening. They sell out quickly. Cash only. Small shop with about 10 seats.

name: Soranoiro
description: Known for their stunning veggie soy milk ramen and colorful presentation. Also has a vegan option. One of the most Instagram-worthy ramen bowls in Tokyo.
whatToOrder: Veggie soy milk ramen or the special golden salt ramen.
tips: Great option for vegetarian travelers. The Tokyo Station branch is more convenient but the original is better.

name: Tsuta
description: The world's first Michelin-starred ramen shop. Their shoyu ramen uses Italian black truffle oil and a complex dashi. Refined and elegant - this is ramen elevated to fine dining.
whatToOrder: Shoyu soba with truffle. Worth the splurge.
tips: Relocated from Sugamo. Check current location and hours before visiting. Reserve online if possible.

name: Sushi Dai
description: Relocated from Tsukiji to Toyosu Market. Serves exceptional omakase sushi at the source - fish goes from the market auction to your plate. The omakase set is legendary.
whatToOrder: Omakase set (chef's choice). Ask for seasonal specials. The tamago (egg) at the end is a perfect finale.
tips: Arrive by 5am to queue. Waits can exceed 3 hours. Go on a weekday. Closed Sundays, Wednesdays and market holidays.

name: Sushi Saito
description: Three Michelin-starred sushi temple. Takashi Saito is considered one of the greatest sushi masters alive. Only 8 seats at the counter. The rice, fish, and technique are unparalleled.
whatToOrder: Omakase only - no choices needed. Let the master work.
tips: Extremely difficult to book - typically requires a concierge at a top hotel to make reservations. Book months in advance. No photos during service.

name: Standing Sushi Nemuro Hanamaru
description: Conveyor belt sushi from Hokkaido with absurdly fresh fish at great prices. Located in the KITTE building near Tokyo Station. The quality rivals much more expensive spots.
whatToOrder: Salmon, ikura (roe), uni (sea urchin), and anything seasonal on the special menu.
tips: Long waits at lunch. Go at 3-4pm for shorter queues. Located in KITTE building 5F near Tokyo Station.
mapsQuery: Nemuro Hanamaru KITTE Tokyo Station sushi

name: Sushi no Midori Shibuya
nameJa: 梅丘寿司の美登利 渋谷店
description: Huge generous cuts of fish at incredibly reasonable prices. The counter seats let you watch the chefs at work. Best value omakase in Shibuya by far.
whatToOrder: The omakase set or the premium sushi platter. The tuna is always outstanding.
tips: In Shibuya Mark City. Take a number and shop while you wait - waits can be 1-2 hours at peak times.
mapsQuery: Sushi no Midori Shibuya Mark City Tokyo

name: Uogashi Nihon-Ichi Standing Sushi
description: Standing sushi bar where you eat at a counter with no seats. Quick, fresh, cheap. Fish comes from Toyosu Market daily. Order piece by piece. The ultimate quick sushi fix.
whatToOrder: Order nigiri piece by piece. Try otoro, engawa, and whatever's seasonal.
tips: No reservations, no waiting - just walk up and order. Perfect for a quick sushi hit. Multiple locations around Tokyo.

name: Toriki
description: Under the Yurakucho train tracks in the atmospheric yakitori alley. Smoke billows, salarymen crowd the counters, trains rumble overhead. This is the Tokyo drinking experience.
whatToOrder: Negima (chicken and leek), tsukune (chicken meatball), and liver. Get a cold beer.
tips: The whole Yurakucho/Shinbashi yakitori alley under the tracks is worth exploring. Cash only at most spots. Go early or late to get a seat.
mapsQuery: Yurakucho yakitori alley under tracks Tokyo

name: Birdland
description: Michelin-starred yakitori in a basement under Ginza. Uses premium Okumikawa chicken. Each skewer is grilled to absolute perfection. The chicken liver pate is legendary. Elevated yakitori at its finest.
whatToOrder: Omakase course. The chicken liver pate and the sasami with wasabi are highlights.
tips: Reservations required. Located in basement of Tsukamoto Sogyo Building. Counter seats offer the best view of the grill master at work.

name: Yakitori Alley (Hoppy Dori)
description: A rowdy open-air street of yakitori joints and bars near Senso-ji. Locals and tourists drink Hoppy (a beer-like beverage) and eat grilled skewers at plastic tables. Pure Tokyo energy.
whatToOrder: Yakitori sets, motsu-ni (stewed offal), and Hoppy (the street's namesake drink).
tips: Multiple stalls to choose from - the busiest ones are usually best. Great afternoon drinking spot. Combine with a Senso-ji visit.

name: Torikizoku
description: Japan's most popular yakitori chain where every item on the menu is ¥360. Massive portions, ice-cold mega highballs, and a rowdy vibe. How salarymen eat after work.
whatToOrder: Everything is ¥360. Get the momo (thigh), kawa (skin), and mega lemon sour highball.
tips: Locations everywhere. Can get packed after 8pm. Perfect for budget drinking and eating. Groups welcome.

name: Tsukiji Outer Market
description: While the inner market moved to Toyosu, the outer market remains a street food paradise. Hundreds of stalls selling tamagoyaki, fresh seafood, wagyu beef skewers, strawberry daifuku, and more.
whatToOrder: Tamagoyaki (sweet egg omelette on a stick), fresh uni, tuna skewers, melon pan, strawberry daifuku.
tips: Go early (before 10am) for the best experience. Most stalls close by 2pm. Eat as you walk. Combine with Tsukiji Hongwanji temple next door.

name: Ameyoko Market
description: A chaotic, vibrant market street running alongside the JR tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi. Stalls hawk fresh seafood, kebabs, chocolate, dried fruits, and cheap street snacks. Electric energy.
whatToOrder: Fresh fruit on sticks, seafood cups, yakitori, and chocolate stalls. Try the ¥500 fresh seafood cups.
tips: Busiest on weekends. Watch for aggressive vendors. Great for browsing and snacking. Not all food stalls are equal - go where locals are lined up.

name: Yanaka Ginza Street Food
description: A retro shopping street with 60+ small shops in Tokyo's old-town. Famous for menchi-katsu (fried meat patties), cat-tail donuts, and nostalgic snacks. Arrive at sunset via the Yuyake Dandan steps.
whatToOrder: Menchi-katsu, cat-tail donuts (nekoshippo), and korokke (croquettes).
tips: Walk from Nippori Station through the atmospheric cemetery. The sunset from Yuyake Dandan steps is legendary. Most shops close by early evening.

name: 7-Eleven Konbini
description: Japanese 7-Eleven is nothing like its American counterpart. Fresh onigiri, egg sandwiches, fried chicken, and seasonal limited items that are genuinely delicious. A pilgrimage for food lovers.
whatToOrder: Egg sandwich (tamago sando), onigiri (tuna mayo is classic), karaage (fried chicken), melon pan, Nanachiki fried chicken.
tips: The egg sandwiches are a cultural phenomenon. Try different onigiri flavors daily. The hot food section has fresh items throughout the day. Seasonal limited items are worth seeking out.

name: Lawson Konbini
description: Lawson's specialty is their fried chicken (Karaage-kun) and premium desserts. Their Uchi Cafe line of sweets rivals actual patisseries. The blue store is your late-night savior.
whatToOrder: Karaage-kun (fried chicken nuggets in multiple flavors), Uchi Cafe premium roll cake, mochi ice cream, Uchi Cafe cheesecake.
tips: Karaage-kun comes in regular, cheese, and seasonal flavors. The premium Uchi Cafe desserts are genuinely excellent. Look for Natural Lawson for healthier upscale options.

name: FamilyMart Konbini
description: FamilyMart's claim to fame is their Famichiki (fried chicken) and excellent Frappe drinks. Their premium bento boxes are a step above. The green and blue store.
whatToOrder: Famichiki (fried chicken fillet), Frappe drinks (caramel, strawberry), premium bento, and the hash browns.
tips: Famichiki is the most popular single item sold at any Japanese konbini. The hot food counter always has fresh items. Their coffee machine is solid.

name: CoCo Ichibanya
description: Japan's #1 curry chain. Customize everything: spice level (1-10), rice amount, and toppings. Comforting Japanese-style curry that's addictive. A guilty pleasure institution.
whatToOrder: Roast chicken cutlet curry, level 3-5 spice. Add cheese topping. ¥300 rice size is enough for most.
tips: Customize spice from 1 (mild) to 10 (pain). Vegetarian options available. Open late. Reliable comfort food anywhere in the city.

name: Yoshinoya
description: The original gyudon (beef bowl) chain since 1899. Sweet soy-braised beef over rice for under ¥500. Fast, cheap, and genuinely satisfying. This is how Japan does fast food.
whatToOrder: Gyudon (beef bowl) regular size with a raw egg on top. Add miso soup.
tips: Open 24 hours at most locations. Perfect ¥4am hunger solution. The raw egg on top of hot rice is the proper way to eat it.

name: Matsuya
description: Yoshinoya's rival with arguably better variety. Their curry is excellent and miso soup comes free with every set. Vending machine ordering makes it zero-stress even without Japanese.
whatToOrder: Premium gyudon set with miso soup (free), or try the curry. Breakfast sets before 10am are great value.
tips: Miso soup is free with any set meal - unbeatable value. Ticket machine ordering. Some locations have premium 'Matsuya Premium' with better ingredients.

name: Kayaba Coffee
description: A beautifully restored 1938 kissaten (old-school coffee shop) in historic Yanaka. The two-story wooden building oozes Showa-era charm. Their egg sandwich and hand-dripped coffee are perfection.
whatToOrder: Tamago sando (egg sandwich) and hand-dripped coffee. The Russian cake is also beloved.
tips: Gets crowded on weekends. The upstairs tatami seating is the best spot. In the heart of Yanaka's nostalgic old-town streets.

name: Chatei Hatou
description: A refined kissaten near Shibuya serving hand-dripped coffee in beautiful vintage cups. Each cup is chosen to match your drink. A serene escape from Shibuya's chaos. Operating since 1989.
whatToOrder: Blend coffee or the café au lait. Each is served in a unique antique cup. Pair with the cheesecake.
tips: No photos of the interior (respectfully). Cash only. The owner selects your cup personally. A meditative experience.

name: Onibus Coffee Nakameguro
nameJa: オニバスコーヒー 中目黒店
description: Third-wave specialty coffee in a tiny renovated house along the Meguro River. Beautiful latte art, single-origin pour-overs, and a chill neighborhood vibe. The terrace is perfect in good weather.
whatToOrder: Flat white or single-origin pour-over. Their espresso is excellent.
tips: Tiny space - you may need to take your coffee to go. Walk along the Meguro River afterward. Multiple locations across Tokyo.

name: Bear Pond Espresso
nameJa: ベアポンドエスプレッソ
description: A legendary espresso bar in bohemian Shimokitazawa. The owner is famously eccentric and the 'angel stain' espresso (available only briefly each day) is considered one of Tokyo's best shots.
whatToOrder: Angel Stain espresso if available (limited times). Otherwise, any espresso drink.
tips: Unpredictable hours - the owner opens when he feels like it. No photos inside. Cash only. Part of the Shimokitazawa experience.

name: Nanaya Aoyama
description: Famous for matcha gelato in 7 levels of intensity. Level 1 is mild, Level 7 is the world's richest matcha ice cream - so concentrated it's almost bitter. A must for matcha lovers.
whatToOrder: Get a double with Level 7 matcha and one other flavor. Level 5 is most popular if you want strong but not extreme.
tips: Small shop, often has a queue. Cash only. Try before committing to Level 7 - it's intensely matcha. The hojicha flavor is also excellent.

name: Dominique Ansel Bakery Omotesando
nameJa: ドミニクアンセルベーカリー
description: The Tokyo outpost of the cronut creator. Japan-exclusive creations that are often better than the NYC original. The made-to-order cookie shot and seasonal specials are phenomenal.
whatToOrder: The cronut (of course), cookie shot, and any Japan-exclusive seasonal items.
tips: Cronuts sell out - go early. The Japan-exclusive items are worth seeking out. Beautiful interior for sitting down.

name: Suzukien Asakusa
description: A tea shop since 1848 collaborating with Nanaya to serve the world's richest matcha gelato. Seven levels of matcha intensity with Level 7 using the highest concentration of matcha available.
whatToOrder: Matcha gelato Level 7 or double scoop to compare levels. Also try their hojicha and black sesame.
tips: Near Senso-ji. The original Asakusa location is more atmospheric than the Aoyama branch. Queue moves quickly.

name: Tempura Kondo
description: Two Michelin-starred tempura from master Fumio Kondo. His signature sweet potato tempura is legendary - sliced thick and fried to sweet, caramelized perfection. Each piece is a revelation.
whatToOrder: Omakase course. The sweet potato and the shrimp are the signatures. Seasonal vegetables are extraordinary.
tips: Reservation required well in advance. Counter seats for the full experience. Lunch is slightly more affordable than dinner.

name: Tendon Tenya
description: Budget tempura chain that punches way above its price point. A full tendon (tempura rice bowl) for under ¥600. Crispy, hot, and surprisingly good for a chain. Perfect quick lunch.
whatToOrder: Regular tendon (tempura rice bowl) at ¥540 is the classic. Upgrade to the Jo (premium) set for extra pieces.
tips: Locations throughout Tokyo. Ticket machine ordering. Quick and no-fuss. Way better than the price suggests.

name: Maisen Tonkatsu
description: Iconic tonkatsu restaurant housed in a converted 1960s bathhouse in Omotesando. The kurobuta (black pork) cutlet is thick, juicy, and the panko coating shatters perfectly. Beautiful interior.
whatToOrder: Kurobuta rosu katsu (black pork loin cutlet) set with unlimited cabbage and rice.
tips: The Omotesando main restaurant (in the old bathhouse) is the one to visit. Grind your own sesame for the sauce. Lunch sets are great value.

name: Butagumi
description: Elevated tonkatsu with a choice of heritage pork breeds. Select your pig by region and breed, each with different flavor profiles. Served with premium rice and homemade pickles.
whatToOrder: Choose a heritage pork variety - the TOKYO X or Kagoshima kurobuta are excellent. The fillet is leaner, loin is fattier.
tips: Reservations recommended for dinner. The pork breed menu can be overwhelming - staff will help you choose. Worth the splurge for pork lovers.

name: Moyan Curry
description: A cult-favorite curry spot with a rich, fruity curry that's been simmered for days. The lunch buffet is insane value - all-you-can-eat curry, rice, and sides. A Shinjuku institution.
whatToOrder: Lunch curry buffet (all-you-can-eat). The beef curry is the flagship. Add cheese topping.
tips: The lunch buffet (11:00-15:00) is the best deal in Shinjuku. Multiple locations. The Shinjuku station area one is most convenient.

name: Harajuku Gyoza Lou
description: A tiny, beloved gyoza specialist in Harajuku. Perfectly crispy on the bottom, juicy inside. Just gyoza, rice, and beer - nothing else needed. Open absurdly late.
whatToOrder: Yaki gyoza (pan-fried) and sui gyoza (boiled). Get both to compare. Add rice and a beer.
tips: Opens until 4am on weekends. Small space - you may wait. Cash only. The simplicity is the point. Some of the best gyoza in Tokyo.

name: Dandasoy Gyoza
description: Craft gyoza with creative fillings beyond the standard pork - think shiso, cheese, and seasonal specials. Modern interior with a fun, casual vibe.
whatToOrder: The sampler plate to try multiple flavors. The shiso gyoza and cheese gyoza are standouts.
tips: Good for groups who want to try many varieties. Beer and gyoza pairing is a joy here.

name: Yoroniku
description: Possibly the best yakiniku in Tokyo. Premium wagyu grilled tableside with stunning presentation. The 'silk rosu' (raw wagyu wrapped around uni and egg yolk) is legendary. Michelin-starred.
whatToOrder: Omakase course. The silk rosu, wagyu tongue, and the special aged cuts are extraordinary.
tips: Reservation essential - book weeks in advance. The omakase is the way to go. Counter seats if available offer the best experience.

name: Gyukatsu Motomura
description: Deep-fried beef cutlet (gyukatsu) that you finish cooking yourself on a hot stone at your table. The outside is crispy, the inside is rare and pink. A unique Tokyo food experience.
whatToOrder: Standard gyukatsu set with barley rice and red miso soup. Dip in the different sauces and wasabi.
tips: The Shinjuku and Shibuya locations have the longest queues. Go at off-peak times. Cook the rare beef on the hot stone to your preferred doneness.

name: Zauo Fishing Restaurant
description: Catch your own fish from an indoor fishing pond, then the kitchen prepares it as sashimi, fried, or grilled. When you catch a fish the whole restaurant cheers. Absurdly fun.
whatToOrder: Whatever you catch! Fishing rod rental included. The sashimi preparation is the most impressive.
tips: Reservations recommended, especially weekends. Located on 1F of Shinjuku Washington Hotel. Fish prices vary - sea bream is the most common catch. Even if you don't catch anything, you can order normally.

name: Omoide Yokocho (Piss Alley)
description: A narrow, atmospheric alley of tiny yakitori and ramen shops near Shinjuku Station's west exit. Smoke, lanterns, and shoulder-to-shoulder seating. This is post-war Tokyo preserved.
whatToOrder: Yakitori, motsu-yaki (grilled offal), and cold beer. Each stall has its own specialty.
tips: Go with an empty stomach and bar-hop between stalls. Most seats 6-10 people. Cash only at most spots. Best experienced at night when the lanterns glow.
mapsQuery: Omoide Yokocho Piss Alley Shinjuku Tokyo

name: Fuji Soba
description: Standing soba noodle chain open 24 hours. Hot soba or udon for under ¥400. The epitome of Japanese fast food - quick, cheap, and satisfying. A 3am essential.
whatToOrder: Tempura soba (soba noodles with a piece of tempura). The curry udon on a cold night.
tips: Standing format - no seats at most locations. Ticket machine ordering. Many locations around major stations. The perfect fuel at any hour.
mapsQuery: Fuji Soba near Shinjuku Station Tokyo

name: Nakajima
description: Michelin-starred kaiseki at lunch for just ¥850. The sardine set lunch is legendary - same kitchen, same quality as the ¥15,000 dinner, at a fraction of the price. Tokyo's greatest lunch deal.
whatToOrder: Lunch: the iwashi (sardine) set at ¥850 is the stuff of legend. Dinner: the kaiseki course.
tips: Arrive by 11:00 to queue for lunch (they open at 11:30, limited sets). The lunch is the famous deal but dinner is world-class kaiseki. In a basement near Shinjuku Station.

name: Den
description: Ranked #20 on World's 50 Best Restaurants. Chef Zaiyu Hasegawa's playful, modern Japanese cuisine includes the famous Dentucky Fried Chicken - a cheeky nod to KFC wrapped in refined technique. Fun and unforgettable.
whatToOrder: Omakase only. The Dentucky Fried Chicken course is the signature experience.
tips: Book months in advance. One of the hardest reservations in Tokyo. The experience is theatrical and joyful - not stuffy. Counter seats recommended.

name: Sometaro
description: A charming, old-school okonomiyaki restaurant in a traditional Japanese house in Asakusa since 1937. You cook your own okonomiyaki on the teppan griddle built into your table.
whatToOrder: Pork okonomiyaki, monjayaki (Tokyo's runny pancake version), and yakisoba.
tips: Cook it yourself - staff will help if you've never made okonomiyaki before. The building itself is a delight. Near Senso-ji.

name: Depachika at Isetan Shinjuku
nameJa: 伊勢丹新宿店 地下食品売場
description: The basement food hall of Isetan department store is a wonderland of premium Japanese cuisine. Hundreds of stalls selling wagashi, bento, pastries, wagyu, and prepared foods. Free samples everywhere.
whatToOrder: Browse everything. Try wagashi (traditional sweets), premium bento boxes, French pastries with Japanese twists, and seasonal specialties.
tips: Go around 6-7pm for discounted bento and items. Free samples are generous. The wagashi section is art. Perfect for assembling a hotel room feast.
mapsQuery: Isetan Shinjuku depachika basement food hall

name: Kikanbo
description: Spicy miso ramen with customizable heat and numbing Sichuan pepper levels. Choose your 'kara' (spice) and 'shibi' (numbing) levels independently. A fiery, addictive bowl.
whatToOrder: Kara-shibi miso ramen. Start with level 3 kara and level 2 shibi if you like spice.
tips: Ticket machine ordering. Be honest about your spice tolerance. The numbness from the Sichuan pepper is intense at higher levels.

name: Udon Shin
description: Hand-made Sanuki-style udon with an incredibly chewy, bouncy noodle. The cold dipping udon is revelatory. A Bib Gourmand spot that's far better than many starred restaurants.
whatToOrder: Curry udon or the cold dipping udon (zaru udon). The tempura sides are excellent.
tips: Small shop near Shinjuku Gyoen. Queue can form at lunch. The noodles are made fresh daily and it shows.

name: Mensho Tokyo
description: Innovative ramen shop known for their lamb ramen, a rare and bold flavor in the ramen world. The lamb broth is surprisingly clean and deeply savory.
whatToOrder: Lamb ramen, lamb tsukemen
tips: Near Tokyo Dome area. The lamb can sell out so go early in each service.

name: Hayashi
description: A niboshi (dried sardine) ramen specialist producing an intensely fishy, umami-packed broth. Beloved by ramen otaku for its uncompromising flavor.
whatToOrder: Niboshi ramen, ajitama topping
tips: Small shop so expect a short wait. The fish flavor is strong, which is the point.

name: Daiwa Sushi
description: The other famous Toyosu Market sushi counter, with a slightly shorter line than Sushi Dai but equally outstanding quality. Fast-paced and exciting counter experience.
whatToOrder: Omakase set, add extra pieces of whatever's seasonal
tips: The line is shorter than Sushi Dai but still long. Go on a weekday if possible.

name: Midori Sushi
description: Exceptional value sushi with large, generous cuts of fish at reasonable prices. Located in Shibuya Mark City with consistently long lines.
whatToOrder: Any set meal, the tuna trio, seasonal fish
tips: Get a ticket number early, then shop in Mark City while waiting. Great quality for the price.

name: Genki Sushi
description: Fun conveyor belt sushi chain where plates are delivered by a small bullet-train system on rails. Budget-friendly and entertaining.
whatToOrder: Order via tablet, try salmon, tuna, shrimp, and tamago
tips: Great for families or casual meals. Order from the tablet for freshly made pieces.

name: Sushi Yoshitake
description: Three-Michelin-star sushi temple in Ginza with extraordinary attention to detail. Chef Yoshitake's rice, aging techniques, and knife work are world-class.
whatToOrder: Omakase only (no menu), trust the chef completely
tips: Reservation required well in advance; try concierge service or hotel booking. Budget 30,000+ yen per person.

name: Andy's Shin Hinomoto
description: Run by a British expat under the Yurakucho train tracks, this raucous izakaya serves fantastic fresh seafood. The atmosphere is electric with trains rumbling overhead.
whatToOrder: Sashimi platter, grilled fish of the day, any seasonal special
tips: Extremely popular with locals and tourists alike. Call ahead or arrive right at opening.

name: Isomaru Suisan
description: 24-hour seafood izakaya chain where you grill your own shellfish at the table. Perfect for late-night seafood cravings any time of day.
whatToOrder: Grilled shellfish set, sashimi, hamachi kama (yellowtail collar)
tips: Open 24 hours, making it a top late-night option. Locations in most entertainment districts.

name: Gonpachi
description: The restaurant that inspired the crazy battle scene in Kill Bill. Dramatic two-story interior with solid yakitori, soba, and izakaya fare.
whatToOrder: Yakitori course, hand-made soba, seasonal tempura
tips: The Nishi-Azabu location is the famous one. Pricier than average but the atmosphere is worth it.

name: Tatemichiya
description: A punk rock izakaya with loud music, tattooed staff, and surprisingly excellent food. The rebellious atmosphere makes for an unforgettable night out.
whatToOrder: Whatever the staff recommends, their creative daily specials
tips: Not for a quiet dinner. Go with friends who want a rowdy, fun experience.

name: Toritama
description: Excellent yakitori spot in Meguro known for high-quality chicken and a warm, welcoming atmosphere. Popular with locals who appreciate serious grilling craft.
whatToOrder: Course menu, chicken sashimi (if you're adventurous), skin
tips: Reserve ahead as it fills up quickly. The chicken sashimi is safe and delicious here.

name: Takeshita Street Crepes
description: Harajuku's famous Takeshita Street is lined with crepe shops serving Japanese-style crepes filled with cream, fruit, and ice cream. A Harajuku icon.
whatToOrder: Strawberry cream crepe, banana chocolate, or matcha cream
tips: Marion Crepes and Santa Monica Crepes are the most popular. Walk and eat is the norm.

name: Nakamise-dori
description: The historic shopping street leading to Senso-ji temple, lined with traditional snack vendors. One of Tokyo's oldest shopping streets with centuries of history.
whatToOrder: Ningyo-yaki (custard cakes), age-manju (fried buns), kibidango (mochi dumplings)
tips: Visit early to avoid the biggest crowds. Combine with a visit to Senso-ji temple.

name: 7-Eleven Egg Sandwich
nameJa: セブンイレブン たまごサンド
description: The iconic fluffy egg sandwich with impossibly soft white bread and creamy egg salad. A must-try that will ruin all other egg sandwiches for you.
whatToOrder: Tamago sando (egg sandwich)
tips: Available at every 7-Eleven. Pair with a can of Boss coffee for peak konbini dining.

name: Lawson Karaage-Kun
nameJa: ローソン からあげクン
description: Bite-sized fried chicken nuggets from the hot food counter at Lawson. Crispy, juicy, and available in regular, red (spicy), and rotating limited-edition flavors.
whatToOrder: Regular flavor first, then try red (spicy) or any limited edition
tips: Check for limited-time seasonal flavors. They sometimes collaborate with anime or regional specialties.

name: FamilyMart Famichiki
nameJa: ファミリーマート ファミチキ
description: FamilyMart's signature fried chicken cutlet, crispy outside and juicy inside. Japan's most popular konbini hot snack, selling hundreds of millions annually.
whatToOrder: Original Famichiki, spicy Famichiki
tips: Best eaten fresh and hot. Pair with a Strong Zero for the ultimate budget Tokyo evening.

name: Lawson Premium Roll Cake
nameJa: ローソン プレミアムロールケーキ
description: An impossibly creamy roll cake from Lawson's premium dessert line that rivals dedicated patisseries. The cream-to-cake ratio is perfection.
whatToOrder: Premium Roll Cake (the original), also try seasonal variations
tips: Check the Lawson dessert section for seasonal limited editions. The original cream version is the essential one.

name: Mos Burger
description: Japan's answer to fast food burgers with higher quality ingredients and unique items like rice burgers. Everything is made to order and tastes noticeably fresher.
whatToOrder: MOS Burger (meat sauce burger), rice burger, spicy MOS cheeseburger
tips: The rice burger (bun made of compressed rice) is uniquely Japanese. Try the seasonal limited items.

name: Saizeriya
description: Absurdly cheap Italian-Japanese family restaurant chain where most dishes are under 500 yen. Wine starts at 100 yen a glass.
whatToOrder: Milan-style doria (gratin), escargot, 100-yen wine, tiramisu
tips: The escargot for 400 yen is an absurd deal. Don't expect authentic Italian, but do expect great value.

name: Cafe de l'Ambre
nameJa: カフェ・ド・ランブル
description: Operating since 1948, this is one of Tokyo's oldest and most revered kissaten. The aged coffee beans and meticulous nel-drip preparation are legendary.
whatToOrder: Aged coffee (ask for their oldest available), nel drip coffee
tips: The late founder aged beans for decades. Ask what aged coffees are available. Cash only.

name: Sarutahiko Coffee
description: Tokyo's beloved specialty coffee chain that helped spark the third-wave coffee movement in Japan. Excellent single-origin pour-overs and espresso drinks.
whatToOrder: Single-origin pour-over, cafe latte, seasonal special
tips: The Ebisu flagship is the original. Also has locations in Omotesando and other areas.

name: Blue Bottle Coffee Japan
nameJa: ブルーボトルコーヒー
description: Blue Bottle's Japan flagship in a converted warehouse is worth visiting for the stunning space alone. The Japanese stores often have exclusive menu items.
whatToOrder: Pour-over, seasonal blend, Japan-exclusive pastries
tips: The Kiyosumi-Shirakawa location is the most beautiful. Combine with a walk around the neighborhood's galleries.

name: Cremia Soft Serve
description: Ultra-premium soft serve ice cream served in a langues de chat cookie cone. Made with 25% fresh Hokkaido cream for an incredibly rich, dense texture.
whatToOrder: Original Cremia soft serve in the cookie cone
tips: Found at various locations and events. The cookie cone alone is worth it. Look for the Cremia sign.
mapsQuery: Cremia soft serve ice cream Tokyo

name: Taiyaki Hiiragi
nameJa: たい焼き ひいらぎ
description: Crispy fish-shaped cakes filled with sweet red bean paste, baked one at a time for maximum crispiness. The thin, crunchy shell sets this shop apart.
whatToOrder: Classic red bean taiyaki, custard cream taiyaki
tips: Best eaten immediately while the shell is still crispy. The thin-style batter is the best in Tokyo.

name: Ethiopia Curry
description: A Kanda curry institution serving fiery Japanese-style curry since the 1980s. Spice levels go up to 70x, but even moderate levels pack serious heat.
whatToOrder: Chicken curry or vegetable curry, start at 5x spice
tips: Kanda/Jimbocho is Tokyo's curry district. Start mild; even 10x is very spicy for most people.

name: Gyoza no Ohsho
description: Japan's biggest gyoza chain serving cheap, satisfying dumplings and Chinese-Japanese dishes. A no-frills institution with hundreds of locations nationwide.
whatToOrder: Gyoza (of course), fried rice, tenshin-han (crab omelette over rice)
tips: Order at least two plates of gyoza per person. The fried rice is also excellent.

name: Dandasadan
description: Trendy gyoza-and-tantanmen chain with a modern, energetic atmosphere. Their crispy gyoza and spicy tantanmen make a perfect combo meal.
whatToOrder: Yaki-gyoza, tantanmen, mazesoba
tips: The combination of gyoza and tantanmen is the move. Multiple locations across Tokyo.

name: Ushigoro
description: Premium yakiniku specializing in A5 wagyu beef with beautiful marbling. Each cut is presented like a work of art and melts on the grill.
whatToOrder: Omakase course, A5 sirloin, wagyu uni sushi, zabuton
tips: Reservations essential. The omakase course is the best way to experience the range of cuts.

name: Stamina-en
description: A legendary yakiniku destination in residential Nerima where people travel from across Tokyo for the best horumon (offal) and premium cuts.
whatToOrder: Mixed horumon (offal), karubi (short rib), harami (skirt steak)
tips: Lines can be 2+ hours on weekends. Go on a weekday. Far from central Tokyo but worth it.

name: Yakiniku Champion
description: High-quality yakiniku in a stylish Ebisu setting with excellent wagyu at more accessible prices than ultra-premium spots. Great date-night option.
whatToOrder: Champion course, thick-cut tongue, wagyu kalbi
tips: Reservations recommended, especially weekends. A solid middle ground between budget and splurge yakiniku.

name: Narisawa
description: Chef Narisawa's innovative 'satoyama cuisine' draws on Japanese nature and sustainability. Dishes like 'Bread of the Forest' with charcoal and soil are thought-provoking.
whatToOrder: Omakase course only, the Bread of the Forest and Essence of the Forest courses
tips: Book well in advance. The philosophy-driven approach makes this more than just a meal.

name: Florilege
description: French-Japanese fine dining with a focus on sustainability and seasonal Japanese ingredients. Counter seats facing Chef Kawate's open kitchen create an intimate experience.
whatToOrder: Omakase course, the Sustainabowl decomposition dish
tips: Reserve through their website well in advance. Counter seats facing the kitchen are the best.

name: Kagaya
description: An absolutely insane izakaya where the owner Mark performs non-stop comedy routines with costumes and props. The food is decent but the show is why you go.
whatToOrder: Whatever Mark suggests, the food is secondary to the experience
tips: Reservations ESSENTIAL and very hard to get. Email well in advance. No photos/video of Mark's show.

name: Alcatraz E.R.
description: A prison-hospital themed izakaya where you're handcuffed, locked in cells, and served drinks in syringes and beakers. Pure campy fun unique to Tokyo.
whatToOrder: Themed cocktails in beakers and test tubes, standard izakaya food
tips: The food is average but that's not the point. Go for the wild atmosphere and themed drinks.

name: Standing Sushi Bar
description: Standing sushi bars found near train stations offer surprisingly high-quality sushi at bargain prices. Eat quickly at the counter and move on.
whatToOrder: Whatever looks fresh in the case, seasonal fish
tips: Look for these near any major station. No reservations, no fuss, just great quick sushi.

name: Uoshin
description: Outstanding seafood izakaya in Shibuya with fish so fresh it rivals sushi restaurants. The handwritten daily menu features whatever was best at the market.
whatToOrder: Sashimi moriawase (assortment), grilled fish, any daily special
tips: Reservations recommended. The daily specials written on the wall are always the way to go.

name: Yakitori Alley (Yurakucho)
description: A collection of smoky yakitori stalls tucked under the Yurakucho rail tracks. Salarymen crowd these tiny counters for cheap, delicious chicken and beer after work.
whatToOrder: Negima (chicken and scallion), kawa (skin), a cold beer
tips: Just wander and pick the stall that looks most appealing. Standing room is common.

name: 7-Eleven Onigiri
nameJa: セブンイレブン おにぎり
description: Perfectly formed rice balls with crispy nori and various fillings. The packaging keeps the seaweed crisp until you unwrap it with a satisfying pull-tab system.
whatToOrder: Tuna mayo (bestseller), salmon, mentaiko (spicy cod roe), umeboshi
tips: Learn the three-step unwrapping technique. Tuna mayo is the safe bet; mentaiko is the adventurous choice.

name: 7-Eleven Melon Pan
nameJa: セブンイレブン メロンパン
description: Sweet bread with a cookie-crust topping shaped to look like a melon. The 7-Eleven version is soft, buttery, and one of the best konbini breads.
whatToOrder: Classic melon pan, or the cream-filled version
tips: Best slightly warmed. Try different brands across all three konbini chains to find your favorite.

name: FamilyMart Frappe
nameJa: ファミリーマート フラッペ
description: Frozen frappe cups that you take to the coffee machine to blend with milk. Available in matcha, chocolate, and seasonal fruit varieties.
whatToOrder: Matcha frappe, chocolate frappe, or seasonal limited flavors
tips: Buy the frozen cup, take it to the coffee machine, press the frappe button. Takes about 30 seconds.
